source: Dr. Aamir's treatment guide (treatment_guide.py), copied word for word
note: Treatment steps name pesticide classes; the portal shows them only once an agronomist has reviewed this file and checked chemical measures against what is registered in Pakistan (#15).

cotton_american_bollworm.name: American Bollworm
symptoms: Round holes bored into squares, flowers, and bolls
Frass (excrement) visible near entry holes
Premature shedding of damaged squares/bolls
treatment_steps: Scout weekly for eggs and small larvae on terminals, squares, and bolls; larvae are easiest to control while young.
Use pheromone traps to monitor adult moth activity and time sprays to egg-hatch peaks.
Conserve natural enemies and consider a Bt-based biological insecticide as a first-line option before broad-spectrum chemicals.
If economic thresholds are exceeded, apply a labeled bollworm insecticide, rotating chemical classes to manage resistance (this pest is prone to developing resistance).
prevention: Where available, use Bt cotton varieties, which carry strong intrinsic resistance to bollworm.
Destroy crop residue after harvest to reduce overwintering pupae.
Avoid excessive nitrogen, which promotes lush growth attractive to egg-laying moths.

cotton_anthracnose.name: Anthracnose
symptoms: Reddish-brown, sunken lesions on bolls, stems, and seedlings
Pink spore masses may appear on lesions in humid weather
Seedling damping-off in severe early infections
treatment_steps: Remove and destroy infected plant debris and bolls after harvest.
Apply a labeled fungicide (e.g. a strobilurin or copper-based product) at early symptom onset, especially during boll development in wet weather.
Improve field drainage and avoid overhead irrigation during boll set.
prevention: Rotate with non-host crops.
Avoid dense planting that keeps the canopy humid.

cotton_aphid.name: Aphid infestation
symptoms: Clusters of small insects on the underside of leaves and new growth
Curled, distorted leaves and sticky honeydew with sooty mould
Sticky lint contamination if aphids are present at boll opening
treatment_steps: Conserve natural predators (ladybird beetles, lacewings) which often control light aphid populations on their own.
Apply a labeled aphicide only if populations exceed the local economic threshold, prioritizing selective products that spare beneficial insects.
Avoid excess nitrogen, which promotes the lush new growth aphids prefer.
prevention: Monitor regularly, especially after any broad-spectrum insecticide application that may have killed natural enemies and triggered a resurgence.

cotton_bacterial_blight.name: Bacterial Blight
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark brown/black and follow the veins
Black lesions on stems ('black arm') and bolls
Premature defoliation and boll rot in severe cases
treatment_steps: Avoid working in wet fields, since the bacteria spread readily via water and equipment.
Apply a copper-based bactericide at early symptom onset; regular fungicides will not work since this is bacterial.
Remove and destroy heavily infected plant debris after harvest.
prevention: Use certified, acid-delinted, disease-free seed -- this disease is strongly seed-borne.
Plant resistant varieties where available.
Rotate with non-host crops for at least one season.

cotton_boll_rot.name: Boll Rot
symptoms: Discolored, decaying bolls that fail to open properly or open with rotted lint
Often follows insect damage (e.g. bollworm entry wounds) or prolonged wet weather
Foul odor and visible fungal growth on affected bolls in advanced stages
treatment_steps: Control boll-feeding insects (bollworm, stink bugs) promptly, since their wounds are the main entry point for boll-rot organisms.
Improve airflow through the canopy (avoid excessive nitrogen and overly dense planting) to reduce humidity around bolls.
Apply a labeled fungicide during boll development if wet weather and disease pressure are both high.
Remove and destroy severely rotted bolls to limit spore spread.
prevention: Manage insect pests proactively rather than reactively.
Avoid excess irrigation/nitrogen late in the season.
Ensure good field drainage.

cotton_healthy.name: Healthy
symptoms: No visible disease or pest symptoms.
treatment_steps: No treatment needed. Continue routine scouting (roughly weekly, more often at squaring/boll stages).
Maintain your regular fertility and irrigation program.
prevention: Keep monitoring for early signs of common cotton pests (thrips, aphids, bollworm, whitefly) and diseases (blight, wilt, anthracnose).

cotton_mealybug.name: Mealybug infestation
symptoms: White, waxy, cottony masses on stems, leaf axils, and bolls
Sticky honeydew and sooty mould on affected plant parts
Stunted growth and boll drop in heavy infestations
treatment_steps: Remove and destroy heavily infested plants/plant parts, especially early in an outbreak, to slow spread.
Conserve natural enemies (parasitic wasps, ladybird beetles), which are often the most effective long-term control.
Apply a labeled systemic insecticide if infestation is severe, since mealybugs' waxy coating resists many contact sprays.
Control ants in the field, as they protect mealybugs from predators in exchange for honeydew.
prevention: Avoid moving infested plant material/equipment between fields.
Remove alternate weed hosts near field borders.

cotton_pink_bollworm.name: Pink Bollworm
symptoms: Pink-colored larvae found inside bolls when opened
Damaged, discolored lint and stained/damaged seed inside affected bolls
Small, rosette-shaped ('rosetted') flowers caused by larvae feeding inside the bud
Premature boll opening or shedding
treatment_steps: Use pheromone traps to monitor adult moth activity and time control action to early egg-hatch -- larvae move inside the boll quickly, where sprays can no longer reach them.
Scout for rosetted flowers and damaged bolls regularly, removing and destroying them to reduce the next generation.
Apply a labeled insecticide timed at egg-hatch/before larvae enter bolls; it's largely ineffective once larvae are inside.
Destroy crop residue and any unopened bolls after the final harvest pick -- larvae overwinter in field trash and stored seed cotton.
prevention: Where available, use Bt cotton varieties with activity against pink bollworm.
Avoid growing a ratoon/second cotton crop, which extends the pest's breeding season.
Keep a clean field break (no standing cotton residue) between seasons.

cotton_red_cotton_bug.name: Red Cotton Bug
symptoms: Clusters of red-and-black bugs (adults and nymphs) on and around fallen bolls, loose seed, and at the base of plants
Staining and quality deterioration of lint and seed from feeding
Mostly a lint/seed-quality issue rather than major direct yield loss
treatment_steps: Collect and destroy fallen bolls, loose seed, and plant debris where the bugs cluster and breed -- sanitation is the most effective single control.
Conserve natural enemies where possible.
Apply a labeled insecticide only if populations are heavy and concentrated; this pest is often manageable through sanitation alone.
prevention: Clear field trash and volunteer cotton plants promptly after harvest.
Avoid leaving picked seed cotton or fallen bolls lying in or near the field.

cotton_thrips.name: Thrips infestation
symptoms: Silvery streaking or stippling on leaves, especially the undersides
Curled, distorted young leaves and stunted seedling growth
Tiny slender insects visible when leaves are shaken over paper
treatment_steps: Scout seedlings closely in the first 3-4 weeks after emergence, when thrips damage is most yield-limiting.
Conserve natural enemies (minute pirate bugs, lacewings) by avoiding unnecessary broad-spectrum sprays.
Apply a labeled thrips insecticide if damage exceeds the local economic threshold, particularly at the seedling stage.
prevention: Avoid planting adjacent to maturing small grains, which push thrips into cotton as they dry down.
chemical_prevention: Consider an at-plant systemic insecticide seed treatment in fields with a history of heavy early thrips pressure.

cotton_whitefly.name: Whitefly infestation
symptoms: Small white flying insects that scatter when plants are disturbed
Yellowing leaves, sticky honeydew, and sooty mould buildup
Whiteflies can also transmit viral diseases (e.g. leaf curl virus)
treatment_steps: Use yellow sticky traps to monitor adult populations.
Conserve natural enemies (parasitic wasps, predatory beetles) and avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum sprays that can trigger resurgence.
Apply a labeled insecticide targeted at whitefly nymphs/adults if populations exceed threshold, rotating modes of action to manage resistance.
prevention: Remove weed hosts and volunteer cotton between seasons.
Avoid planting near other whitefly-prone crops when possible.
Use reflective or UV-blocking mulches in high-value plantings if locally practiced.

cotton_wilt.name: Wilt (Fusarium/Verticillium)
symptoms: Yellowing and wilting of leaves, often starting on one side of the plant or lower leaves first
Vascular discoloration (brown streaking) visible when the stem is cut lengthwise
Stunted growth and eventual plant death in severe cases
treatment_steps: There is no effective in-season cure for vascular wilt -- management is primarily preventive and long-term.
Remove and destroy severely wilted plants to reduce soil inoculum buildup.
Improve field drainage, since waterlogged/compacted soils worsen wilt severity.
Avoid working in infected fields and then healthy fields without cleaning equipment, since soil-borne fungi spread via contaminated tools/machinery.
prevention: Plant wilt-resistant/tolerant varieties -- this is the single most effective control.
Rotate with non-host crops (e.g. cereals) for several years in infected fields.
Maintain balanced soil fertility and avoid plant stress, which increases susceptibility.

maize_armyworm.name: Armyworm (Fall Armyworm)
symptoms: Ragged, window-pane feeding damage on young leaves, often in the whorl
Sawdust-like frass packed in the leaf whorl
Large numbers of caterpillars can strip a field rapidly, moving 'like an army'
treatment_steps: Scout the whorl of young plants regularly -- catching larvae while small (early instars) is far more effective than treating large larvae.
Handpick and destroy egg masses and young larvae in small plantings if feasible.
Conserve natural enemies (parasitic wasps, birds) where possible.
If populations exceed threshold, apply a labeled insecticide targeted at the whorl, timed for early larval stages; rotate modes of action since fall armyworm develops resistance quickly.
prevention: Plant early within the recommended local window to reduce overlap with peak moth flights.
Where available, use Bt maize varieties with activity against fall armyworm.
Monitor with pheromone traps to catch outbreaks early.

maize_common_rust.name: Common Rust
symptoms: Small, round to elongated cinnamon-brown pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces
Pustules turn dark brown/black as they age
Severe infection causes leaf yellowing and premature death
treatment_steps: Scout regularly, especially in cool, humid weather which favors this fungus.
Apply a triazole or strobilurin-class fungicide if pustules are found before/around tasseling on a susceptible variety, since this is the period when yield loss risk is highest.
A single well-timed application is often sufficient; repeat only if disease pressure remains high afterward.
prevention: Plant common-rust-resistant hybrids -- resistance is widely available and highly effective.
Avoid very early planting in cool, high-humidity regions where rust pressure is historically high.

maize_ear_rot.name: Ear Rot
symptoms: Moldy, discolored kernels on the ear (pink, white, grey, or black fungal growth depending on the fungus involved)
Husks may stick tightly to the ear or show premature drying
Potential mycotoxin contamination in badly rotted ears
treatment_steps: Harvest promptly at maturity and dry grain quickly -- these fungi thrive in damp, warm conditions, so slow drying makes rot worse.
Remove and discard visibly rotted ears/kernels rather than storing or feeding them.
If a labeled foliar fungicide is used, timing it around silking is most effective for reducing infection risk.
Segregate and test grain for mycotoxins before it enters food/feed channels if rot was significant.
prevention: Use resistant hybrids where available.
Manage ear-feeding insects (e.g. earworm, borers), since insect wounds are a common entry point for these fungi.
Ensure good field drainage and avoid drought/heat stress during grain fill, which increases susceptibility.
Store harvested grain at low moisture in clean, dry conditions.

maize_fall_armyworm.name: Fall Armyworm
symptoms: Ragged, window-pane feeding damage on young leaves, often in the whorl
Sawdust-like frass packed in the leaf whorl
Large numbers of caterpillars can strip a field rapidly
treatment_steps: Scout the whorl of young plants regularly -- catching larvae while small (early instars) is far more effective than treating large larvae.
Handpick and destroy egg masses and young larvae in small plantings if feasible.
Conserve natural enemies (parasitic wasps, birds) where possible.
If populations exceed threshold, apply a labeled insecticide targeted at the whorl, timed for early larval stages; rotate modes of action since fall armyworm develops resistance quickly.
prevention: Plant early within the recommended local window to reduce overlap with peak moth flights.
Where available, use Bt maize varieties with activity against fall armyworm.
Monitor with pheromone traps to catch outbreaks early.

maize_gray_leaf_spot.name: Gray Leaf Spot
symptoms: Narrow, rectangular tan-to-gray lesions running parallel to leaf veins
Lesions can coalesce and cause extensive leaf blighting, starting on lower leaves
Worse in continuous maize with reduced tillage (fungus survives on residue)
treatment_steps: Apply a triazole or strobilurin-class fungicide around tasseling if lesions are present on leaves near/above the ear leaf, since protecting the upper canopy is most important for yield.
Improve residue decomposition (light tillage) in high-pressure, continuous-maize fields.
Increase row spacing/reduce plant density slightly in chronically high-pressure fields to improve airflow.
prevention: Plant resistant/tolerant hybrids -- this is the most cost-effective long-term control.
Rotate with a non-host crop (e.g. soybean, wheat) for at least one season.
Manage crop residue rather than leaving heavy surface trash in no-till continuous maize.

maize_healthy.name: Healthy
symptoms: No visible disease or pest symptoms.
treatment_steps: No treatment needed. Continue routine scouting through tasseling and grain fill.
Maintain your regular fertility and irrigation program.
prevention: Keep monitoring for early signs of common maize issues (rust, gray leaf spot, armyworm/fall armyworm).

maize_stem_borer.name: Stem Borer
symptoms: Rows of small round holes across young leaves, from larvae feeding before the whorl unfurls
'Deadheart' -- a dead central shoot in young plants that pulls out easily
Tunnels visible inside the stem when split open; broken/lodged stems in older plants
treatment_steps: Scout the whorl of young plants regularly for pinhole feeding damage -- this is the easiest stage to catch it, before larvae bore into the stem.
Remove and destroy visibly infested/deadheart plants to reduce carryover.
Apply a labeled insecticide into the whorl if infestation is caught early; once larvae are inside the stem, sprays are far less effective.
Conserve natural enemies (parasitic wasps) where possible.
prevention: Destroy old maize stalks/residue after harvest -- larvae overwinter inside old stems.
Where available, use Bt maize hybrids with activity against stem borers.
Avoid late or staggered planting, which extends the pest's breeding window.

rice_bacterial_blight.name: Bacterial Leaf Blight
symptoms: Water-soaked streaks starting at leaf tips/margins that turn yellow then grey-white
Wavy lesion margins running along the veins
Milky bacterial ooze visible on cut leaves in early morning ('Kresek' wilting in seedlings)
treatment_steps: Drain standing water where possible -- the disease spreads readily through water and wind-driven rain.
Avoid working in or irrigating infected fields when foliage is wet, to reduce mechanical spread.
Apply a copper-based bactericide or a product specifically labeled for bacterial blight if pressure is high; fungicides are NOT effective since this is bacterial, not fungal.
Remove and destroy severely infected plants/tillers.
prevention: Use resistant varieties -- this is the most effective long-term control for bacterial blight.
Avoid excess nitrogen, which increases susceptibility.
Use clean, pathogen-free seed and avoid clipping seedling tops before transplanting (a common infection entry point).

rice_blast.name: Rice Blast
symptoms: Diamond/spindle-shaped lesions with grey centers and brown margins on leaves
Neck/node infection causes the panicle to snap or fail to fill ('neck blast')
Rapid spread under warm, humid, cloudy conditions with heavy nitrogen use
treatment_steps: Drain and dry the field briefly if feasible, since blast favors continuously wet, humid canopies.
Apply a labeled fungicide (e.g. tricyclazole or strobilurin class) at first leaf symptoms, and again at booting/heading if neck blast risk is high.
Reduce nitrogen top-dressing; split nitrogen applications rather than one heavy dose.
Remove and destroy heavily infected plant debris after harvest.
prevention: Use certified seed and blast-resistant varieties recommended for your area.
Avoid excessive seedling density and nitrogen.
Maintain balanced potassium and silicon nutrition, which strengthens plant resistance.

rice_brown_spot.name: Brown Spot
symptoms: Small, round to oval brown lesions with a grey/white center on leaves and grains
Often associated with nutrient-poor or stressed soils (especially potassium deficiency)
Discolored, spotted grains at harvest ('dirty panicle')
treatment_steps: Correct soil fertility, especially potassium deficiency, which strongly predisposes rice to brown spot.
Apply a labeled fungicide (e.g. a triazole or mancozeb-class product) if disease pressure is high, particularly around flowering to protect grain quality.
Improve field drainage and avoid water stress.
prevention: Use healthy, disease-free seed -- brown spot is significantly seed-borne.
Balance fertilization (N-P-K) rather than relying on nitrogen alone.
Practice crop rotation and residue management.

rice_tungro.name: Tungro (viral disease)
symptoms: Yellow-orange leaf discoloration, starting at the tip
Stunted growth and reduced tillering
Delayed or incomplete flowering
treatment_steps: There is no curative treatment for a virus -- management focuses entirely on controlling the green leafhopper vector and removing infected plants.
Rogue out (remove) infected plants early to reduce the source of virus for leafhoppers to spread.
If leafhopper populations are high, apply a labeled insecticide targeted at the vector rather than the virus itself, following resistance-management rotation.
Avoid staggered planting dates in a local area, which lets leafhoppers move continuously between young and mature crops.
prevention: Plant tungro-resistant/tolerant varieties where available.
Synchronize planting dates with neighboring farms to create a 'clean' break in host availability.
Avoid continuous rice cropping without a fallow period in high-incidence areas.

sugarcane_healthy.name: Healthy
symptoms: No visible disease or pest symptoms.
treatment_steps: No treatment needed. Continue routine monitoring (roughly weekly) so any new symptoms are caught early.
Maintain balanced fertilization and irrigation scheduling appropriate for your growth stage.
prevention: Keep scouting regularly, since early detection is the biggest factor in successful disease/pest management.
Maintain field sanitation (clean equipment, certified planting material) to keep disease pressure low.

sugarcane_mosaic.name: Mosaic
symptoms: Mottled light-green and dark-green patches on leaves (a mosaic pattern)
Most visible on younger, actively growing leaves
Stunted growth and reduced stalk/sugar yield in heavily infected plants
treatment_steps: There is no curative treatment for a virus -- management focuses on removing infected plants and controlling the aphid vector.
Rogue out and destroy clearly symptomatic clumps to reduce the source of virus for aphids to spread further.
If aphid populations are high, apply a labeled insecticide targeted at the vector, since aphids are what carry the virus between plants.
prevention: Use certified, virus-indexed (virus-free) seed cane rather than setts taken from unverified stalks.
Plant mosaic-resistant/tolerant varieties where available.
Avoid propagating planting material from any stalk showing mosaic symptoms.

sugarcane_red_rot.name: Red Rot
symptoms: Reddish discoloration inside the stalk with white cross-bands when cut open
Withering and drying of leaves, often starting with the top leaves
Sour, alcoholic smell from infected, rotting stalks
treatment_steps: Rogue out and destroy (burn, don't compost) severely infected clumps to reduce disease spread within the field.
Avoid using seed cane (setts) from infected fields for future planting -- this disease spreads heavily through infected planting material.
Improve field drainage, since waterlogging increases red rot severity.
Where infection is caught very early, a fungicidal sett (seed piece) treatment before planting can help reduce transmission in future crops.
prevention: Plant certified, disease-free sett material, ideally from a resistant variety.
Rotate out of sugarcane for a season in fields with a history of severe red rot.
Avoid mechanical injury to stalks (from cultivation equipment, rodents) which creates entry points for the fungus.

sugarcane_red_rust.name: Red Rust
symptoms: Small, elongated orange-to-reddish-brown pustules, mainly on the leaf underside
Pustules rupture the leaf surface, releasing rust-colored spores that rub off on your hand
Heavy infection causes premature yellowing and drying of leaves, reducing photosynthesis
treatment_steps: Remove and destroy severely infected leaves/trash to reduce spore load in the field.
Apply a labeled triazole or strobilurin fungicide if pustules are widespread and warm, humid weather is likely to keep favoring spread.
Avoid dense planting and excess nitrogen, which keep the canopy humid and favor rust development.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant varieties where available -- this is the most effective long-term control.
Ensure adequate row spacing for airflow through the canopy.
Maintain balanced fertilization rather than heavy nitrogen alone.

sugarcane_yellow_rust.name: Yellow Rust
symptoms: Small yellow-to-orange pustules on leaves, often clustered in streaks
Most damaging on younger leaves under warm, humid conditions
Premature yellowing and drying of heavily infected leaves
treatment_steps: Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves where practical.
Apply a labeled triazole or strobilurin fungicide if pustules are widespread and conditions remain favorable for spread.
Improve field drainage and avoid waterlogging, which stresses the crop and worsens disease severity.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant varieties where available.
Maintain balanced fertilization; avoid excess nitrogen.
Avoid dense planting that keeps the canopy humid.

wheat_aphid.name: Aphid infestation
symptoms: Clusters of small green/black insects on leaves, stems, and ear heads
Curled, yellowing, or sticky (honeydew-covered) leaves
Sooty mould growing on honeydew residue
treatment_steps: Scout fields weekly from tillering through grain-fill; check the underside of leaves and ear heads.
Encourage natural predators (ladybird beetles, lacewings, parasitic wasps) by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticide sprays unless the economic threshold is exceeded.
If aphid counts exceed your region's action threshold, apply a labeled aphicide (e.g. a pyrethroid or neonicotinoid) at the recommended rate, ideally targeting early infestation.
Rotate insecticide modes of action between sprays to slow resistance buildup.
Remove volunteer wheat and grassy weeds near fields, which host aphids between seasons.
prevention: Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which promotes lush growth aphids favor.
Plant early where feasible so the crop outgrows peak aphid pressure.
Use aphid-tolerant varieties if available locally.

wheat_black_rust.name: Black (Stem) Rust
symptoms: Elongated, reddish-brown to black pustules on stems, leaves, and leaf sheaths
Pustules rupture the epidermis and can be felt as raised, rough patches
Lodging (stem breakage) in severe infections
treatment_steps: Remove and destroy volunteer wheat and barberry (the alternate host) near fields where possible.
Apply a triazole or strobilurin-class foliar fungicide at first sign of pustules, and repeat per label interval if conditions stay warm and humid.
Prioritize spraying if disease is detected before flag-leaf emergence, since stem rust can cause major yield loss if it reaches the stem/head stage untreated.
Avoid dense planting and excess nitrogen, which increase canopy humidity.
prevention: Plant resistant/tolerant wheat varieties recommended for your region.
Practice crop rotation with non-cereal crops.
Monitor regional rust forecasts/alerts if your agriculture department publishes them.

wheat_brown_rust.name: Brown (Leaf) Rust
symptoms: Small, round to oval orange-brown pustules scattered on the upper leaf surface
Pustules are smaller and more randomly scattered than yellow rust's striped pattern
Premature yellowing and drying of leaves in heavy infections
treatment_steps: Scout regularly from stem elongation onward, especially in humid, mild weather (15-22°C).
Apply a triazole (e.g. propiconazole/tebuconazole-class) or strobilurin fungicide once pustules are found on the upper leaves, particularly if the flag leaf is still healthy and worth protecting.
A second spray may be needed 2-3 weeks later if conditions remain favorable for the fungus.
Destroy volunteer wheat plants that can carry the fungus between seasons.
prevention: Choose leaf-rust resistant varieties where available.
Avoid late/very dense sowing which extends the favorable infection window.

wheat_flag_smut.name: Flag Smut
symptoms: Leaves show long, narrow, black/grey streaks running parallel to the veins
Streaks rupture to release black powdery spore masses
Twisted, stunted plants that often fail to produce a normal head
treatment_steps: Remove and destroy infected plants where feasible to reduce soil spore load.
Treat seed with a systemic fungicide seed treatment before sowing in future seasons -- this is the primary control point since the fungus is seed- and soil-borne.
Avoid using seed saved from an infected field.
prevention: Rotate out of wheat for 2-3 years in fields with a history of flag smut.
Plant resistant varieties where available.

wheat_healthy.name: Healthy
symptoms: No visible disease or pest symptoms.
treatment_steps: No treatment needed. Continue routine scouting through stem elongation, flowering, and grain fill.
Maintain your regular fertility and irrigation program.
prevention: Keep monitoring for early signs of common wheat rusts, mildew, and aphid/mite pressure.

wheat_leaf_blight.name: Leaf Blight
symptoms: Irregular brown-to-tan lesions on leaves, often with yellow margins
Lesions may coalesce, causing large areas of leaf death
Reduced grain fill from loss of photosynthetic leaf area
treatment_steps: Remove and destroy infected crop debris after harvest rather than leaving it on the soil surface.
Apply a broad-spectrum foliar fungicide (triazole or strobilurin class) at early symptom onset, especially at flag-leaf stage when protecting the top leaves matters most.
Improve field drainage and avoid overhead irrigation late in the day, since prolonged leaf wetness favors the fungus.
prevention: Rotate with non-cereal crops for at least one season.
Use certified, disease-free seed and resistant varieties where available.
Avoid excess nitrogen which creates a dense, humid canopy.

wheat_mite.name: Mite infestation
symptoms: Fine stippling or silvery/bronze discoloration on leaves
Leaves may curl or dry out under heavy infestation
Tiny moving specks visible on leaf undersides with a hand lens
treatment_steps: Confirm mites (not another cause of stippling) with a hand lens or by shaking leaves over white paper.
Encourage predatory mites and insects by minimizing unnecessary insecticide use, which can flare mite populations by killing natural enemies.
If populations are heavy, apply a labeled miticide; note that many general insecticides do NOT control mites effectively.
Manage field-edge grassy weeds that can harbor mites between seasons.
prevention: Avoid moisture stress in the crop, since drought-stressed wheat is more susceptible to mite buildup.
Monitor closely during hot, dry spells when mite reproduction accelerates.

wheat_powdery_mildew.name: Powdery Mildew
symptoms: White to greyish powdery fungal growth on leaves, stems, and sometimes ear heads
Yellowing and premature death of affected leaves
Most common in dense canopies with poor air circulation
treatment_steps: Improve canopy airflow by avoiding overly dense seeding rates.
Apply a triazole or specific powdery-mildew-targeted fungicide once white patches are observed, particularly before flag-leaf infection.
Reduce nitrogen top-dressing if the canopy is unusually lush and dense.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties where available -- powdery mildew resistance genes are common in modern wheat breeding.
Avoid continuous wheat-on-wheat cropping in high-pressure fields.

wheat_scab.name: Scab / Fusarium Head Blight
symptoms: Bleached, tan spikelets on an otherwise green head (premature ripening in patches)
Pink or orange fungal growth at the base of infected spikelets in humid weather
Shriveled, discolored ('tombstone') kernels; potential mycotoxin (DON) contamination
treatment_steps: Apply a triazole fungicide labeled for Fusarium head blight timed at flowering (anthesis) -- this is the critical, narrow window for effective control; sprays before or well after flowering are far less effective.
Because scab-affected grain can carry mycotoxins, segregate and test harvested grain before it enters food/feed channels if infection was significant.
Rotate away from wheat/maize and manage residue, since the fungus survives on cereal stubble.
prevention: Use scab-tolerant varieties where available.
Avoid planting wheat directly into maize or wheat stubble without tillage/residue management.
Monitor regional scab risk forecasts around flowering time if available.

wheat_stem_fly.name: Stem Fly infestation
symptoms: Dead central shoot ('deadheart') that pulls out easily in young plants
White, chaffy, empty ear heads ('whiteheads') at later growth stages
Small maggots may be found inside affected stems
treatment_steps: Remove and destroy affected tillers (deadhearts/whiteheads) to reduce carryover of larvae.
If infestation is detected early (seedling stage), a labeled systemic insecticide seed treatment or early foliar spray can reduce damage.
Time sowing to avoid the fly's peak egg-laying period in your region if local extension guidance provides this window.
prevention: Avoid very early or staggered sowing dates that overlap with fly activity peaks.
Destroy volunteer wheat and grassy weed hosts after harvest.

wheat_yellow_rust.name: Yellow (Stripe) Rust
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange pustules arranged in narrow stripes along the leaf veins
Stripes are a key distinguishing feature versus the scattered pustules of brown/black rust
Severe infection causes leaf yellowing, drying, and yield loss
treatment_steps: Scout fields regularly in cool, humid weather (10-15°C is highly favorable for this fungus).
Apply a triazole or strobilurin fungicide as soon as stripe symptoms are confirmed, prioritizing protection of the flag leaf.
A follow-up spray may be needed if cool, wet weather persists.
Destroy volunteer wheat that can carry the pathogen between seasons.
prevention: Plant yellow-rust resistant varieties -- resistance can break down over time as new pathogen races emerge, so check current regional recommendations.
Avoid very early sowing in high-risk zones.
